families.s: HSE work-equipment maintenance, isolation and lock-off guidance
families.t: planned maintenance, competence, shutdown, stored energy, isolation, lock-off, permits, hot work and return to service
f: Maintenance should be planned and carried out by competent people with suitable information and training.
Equipment should normally be shut down and isolated before maintenance, cleaning, adjustment or blockage removal.
High-risk equipment may require positive disconnection and lock-off to prevent inadvertent reconnection.
Stored electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, gravitational, thermal and mechanical energy must be released or secured.
Mobile plant may require neutral selection, parking brakes and wheel chocks.
Formal permit-to-work systems may be required for high-risk maintenance.
Vessels and equipment containing flammable or toxic materials require cleaning, checking and specialist controls before hot work or entry.
Guards, controls and safety devices must be restored and tested before equipment returns to service.
families.g: Isolation effectiveness depends on every energy source, stored energy, lock ownership, verification, communication, contractor interfaces, testing and controlled restoration.

families.s: HSE woodworking-machinery guarding and safe-use guidance
families.t: PUWER application, dangerous-part guarding, braking, tooling, training, authorised use, extraction, maintenance and isolation
f: The woodworking-machinery ACOP applies to most fixed woodworking machinery used on wood and composite materials.
Access to dangerous moving parts must be prevented by suitable fixed, interlocked or other protective measures.
Only trained and authorised people should use machines presenting specific risks.
Information and training must cover normal use, adjustments, cleaning, tool changing and foreseeable faults.
Risk assessment resources address high-risk hand-fed machines including circular saws, band saws, planers and spindle moulders.
Braking may be necessary to reduce hazardous run-down time before access.
Wood dust and chips should be controlled through suitable extraction and housekeeping.
Maintenance and blockage clearance require effective isolation and restoration of guards before restart.
families.g: Woodworking-machine risk depends on machine and cutter, guarding, feed, braking, tooling, workpiece, extraction, run-down, isolation, competence and production pressure.

families.s: HSE sawmill machinery, transport and lock-out guidance
families.t: blade and pulley cleaning, timber stacking, cross-cut saws, site transport, lock-out, noise, welfare and supervision
f: Sawmilling remains a high-risk industry with machinery accidents a major cause of serious injury.
High-risk activities include band-saw blade or pulley cleaning and power-operated cross-cut saws.
Round and sawn timber stacking must prevent collapse and uncontrolled movement.
Site-transport routes and loading activities require planned separation and control.
Lock-out procedures are required when interrupting mechanised production, including freeing jammed timber.
Machine guards and safety-critical devices must remain effective and be restored after maintenance.
Noise exposure should be assessed and reduced through machinery, enclosure and work-organisation controls.
Adequate welfare, housekeeping, competence and supervision support safe sawmill operation.
families.g: Sawmill risk depends on machinery, timber movement and stacking, automated sequences, lock-out, transport, noise, housekeeping, maintenance and worker competence.

families.s: HSE printing-press, guillotine and paper-converting machinery guidance
families.t: guarding, interlocks, limited movement, operator training, daily checks, maintenance, solvents, health surveillance and older machinery
f: Printing machinery presents hazards from moving presses, in-running nips, cutters, knives and paper-converting mechanisms.
Power-operated guillotine operators require training in hazards, controls, safeguards, safe practice and daily checks.
Printing presses need safeguards appropriate to their design, age and operating modes.
Cutting machines require controls that prevent access to hazardous knife and moving-part zones.
Guards removed for cleaning or maintenance must be replaced and safety features checked before operation.
Safety-critical guards and protective devices need planned preventative or condition-based maintenance.
Inks, solvents, adhesives and cleaning products may create respiratory, skin, fire and explosion risks.
Health surveillance may be required where respiratory sensitisers or skin hazards remain after controls.
families.g: Printing risk depends on machine type and age, safeguards, operating mode, cleaning and maintenance, chemicals, ventilation, competence, production speed and surveillance.
